teaching: The esoteric interpretation of 'la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-'aliy al-'azim' is that hawl is Mawlana Hasan, quwwah is Mawlana Husayn, and Ali al-Azim is greater than both.

The Prophet's hadith 'al-Hasanu wa al-Husaynu Imama haqqin qama aw qa'ada wa abuhuma khayrun minhuma' establishes that Hasan and Husayn are both Imams of truth whether they rise or sit, and their father Ali is better than both.
Because the ma'rifat of Allah cannot be attained, the gnosis of the spiritual and physical hudud is the necessary path, and one's recognition must be correct from the Imam down to where one sits.
A human being comes into existence gradually through the dawla-e-alam, traversing mineral, plant, and animal forms before reaching the human form, whether in descent (tanazzul) or ascent (taraqqi).
The human is brought to a standard point (khawand-e-alifiyyah) and presented the guiding mission (da'wat-e-hadiyah); accepting it settles his matter, rejecting it means descent.
The Tenth Intellect (ashir-e-mudabbir, mudabbir-e-ka'inat) intended to lift the fallen world through two paths only: through man (becoming ashraf al-makhluqat) and through nasut and lahut.
Nasut is that which has physicality and density (kathafat) — the visible Imam, also called Imam-e-Mubin, ghilaf, or simply Imam.
Lahut is that which is unseen and is greater than nasut, designated by the three terms imamat, haykal, and lahut.
Nasut has graded stages (madarij): zilli (shadowy), tabi'i (natural), and khass (special).
Nasut-e-tabi'i is formed from the rihiyyat of the believers of the islands (jaza'ir), and upon it fall all the calamities and difficulties that befall the Imam.
Nasut-e-zilli is higher and unseen, formed from the higher hudud and afadil, and its guardian is Umm al-Dhakr, the mother of the Imam.
The mother of every Imam is the wife of another Imam, and these chaste women (batulat) are so pure that some of them are greater than the prophets (excluding the Prophet Muhammad).
Nasut-e-khass is the highest unseen stage, not originating in this world, formed from the hudud of the hudarat (the high du'at) who are pure from the beginning.
Rihiyyat is defined as baqaya al-namiyah, the remnant of the vegetative faculty that remains in a believer at death and, emerging after three days, is renamed rihiyyah, like a fragrance or wind.

The rihiyyat ascends from the moon through Mercury, Venus, the sun, and Jupiter, returns to reside in the moon, and when the Imam intends a successor it descends via signals from the amud al-nur into the hudarat, which the Imam and his wife consume to conceive the future Imam.
There is an ascending hierarchy of subtle matter: fudulat (waste) below rihiyyat below sughrat (the concept/tasawwur), and the ascent in prayer (salat) is on account of this refinement.
The sughrat is one's creed and concept about religion, the highest thing, which emerges as the spiritual form (surat-e-ruhani) and is the only true capital a person carries from this world.
Nasut-e-kulli is a stage higher than nasut-e-khass, granted only to certain specific Imams, being the combined essence of various Imams.
Lahut and nasut are the two ladders of progress — the physical ascends through nasut and the spiritual through lahut — and within lahut is imamat.

The rational soul (nafs-e-natiqah) is not of this world but came at the moment of the oath of allegiance (ahd), when the leaven of regret (khamir-e-nadamat) is first received upon naming the Imam, and it must be continually increased.
At death the rational soul pulls the sensory faculty (hissiyyah, the 'I'/self) upward, and one's deeds — zakat, fasts, Hajj — bundle together into the spiritual form (surat-e-ruhani).

The spiritual form rises to one's higher rank (hadd-e-ali) and proceeds step by step through successive hadd-e-ali to the bab al-abwab and then the Imam — a concept exclusive to the followers of the Ahl al-Bayt.

The believer's spark received at the oath is like a coal that deeds fan into an ember while neglect dims it toward extinction, and at death the Imam al-Zaman judges its state and may grant intercession (shafa'at) to rekindle it.
Supplications for the deceased seek that Allah include him in the group of the Prophet and the progeny of Muhammad so he may be elevated past the valleys where souls otherwise get stuck.
The hur al-'in promised to the believer is his own spiritual form (surat-e-ruhani); to meet the hur al-'in is to see one's surat-e-ruhani at death.

At the time of death a person sees the forms of Mawlana Ali, the Prophet, the Imam of each era, and his own benefactor or teacher (hadd-e-ali), and the radiance on the dying face is from beholding these forms.
Believers are of differing types (lawahid) according to the scale on which their lahut was arranged — whether by shari'at alone, by ta'wil, or by haqa'iq.
Hu is the level at which the Lord of the Worlds created the spiritual realm (alam-e-ruhani); there is no question and answer there, and nothing is known of what preceded it.
Literally, Allah means that regarding which one falls into amazement (hayrat) or for which one feels longing (shawq); since worship is rendered only to Hu, the worship done is for Hu.

The cosmos is layered upward from the physical realm (alam-e-jismani, lowest dense matter) to the luminous celestial realm (jirmani alam / falakiyat) to the Realm of Command (alam-e-amr / ijad / ghayb) to the spiritual realm which is the alam of Hu, containing ten principles and the ten intellects.
The number ten holds a special status, corresponding to the ten intellects arranged in the spiritual realm.
The primordial mistake was made by the Second Emanation (Munba'ith-e-Thani, also called Tali), who consequently became the Tenth Intellect (Aql-e-Ashir).

The entire material world was created as the atonement for the Second Emanation's mistake, formed from the disobedient and fallen ones; without that error there would be no world, only the realm of purity (alam of shafa').
The First Emanation (Munba'ith-e-Awwal) followed the First Intellect correctly, whereas the Second Emanation erred.

The First Intellect (Aql-e-Awwal), without any teacher, imitated and led, becoming the most excellent (afdal-tarin) and victorious (fa'iz) being though still a servant (bandah) with no equal — the Preceder (Sabiq).
The First Intellect is the Exalted Originator (Mubdi' Ta'ala) and bears the names Sabiq-e-Awwal, Mawjud-e-Awwal, and Wujud-e-Awwal, a different name for each status.
The error of the Second Intellect was to declare 'I and my companion are equal'; since there is no equality in ranks, this claim of equality caused the fall.
Density (kathafat) arose through the absence of light (adam-e-nur), since darkness is not a thing in itself but merely the privation of nur.
After the fall the disobedient immediately repented; seven intellects descended, and the eighth that came became the Tenth Intellect.
Tawhid is the highest and most exalted chapter and cannot be grasped by the intellect; that which does not come into understanding is our Allah, for if it could be understood it would not be Allah.

Ability (istita'at) only operates through obedience (ta'at): as a tasbih bead has the capacity to rise but does not rise until raised by another, no one becomes great by himself but only when a great one makes him so.
Understanding the ranks (marathib) is the very meaning of religion (din).

The eras descend in transparency: the current dense era (kathif alam, a time of difficulties) below the nafsani alam, below the jirmani alam, below the wholly transparent realm of unveiling (alam of kashf); fitrat means the shrinkage of nature into laziness.
Doubt (shakk) nullifies religious acts — prayer, ablution, and all else remain incomplete with doubt — and only certainty (yaqin) completes them.

Intention (niyyat) is the most important element of worship, requiring affirmation by the heart and utterance by the tongue (tasdiq bi'l-jinan wa qawl bi'l-lisan); without proper intention the spiritual beings do not act and prayer becomes mere bodily motion like yoga.
The Prophet's hadith 'sataftariqu ummati 'ala thalathin wa sab'ina firqatan' foretells that his community will divide into seventy-three sects, one of which is saved (naji) and the rest hell-bound.
The esoteric meaning of the seventy-three sects is the changing of intentions during the fall from top to bottom, as souls passed through states of kufr, shirk, doubt, and following.
The sect of the repentant (firqat al-nadimin) is the most excellent, and the Tenth Intellect / Second Emanation, the first to repent, is called the Spiritual Adam (Adam-e-Ruhani).

The four elements (arkan: fire, water, air, earth) were created from those who fell into amazement (the doubtful, shakkin), and the lower world beneath the earth's surface was made from the insistent and arrogant (musirr and mustakbirin).
Mastership (mawlayat) begins at the point where one falls into amazement, and that is Allah; ilah is a separate, lesser term denoting what the disbelievers fabricate.

Within creation the hierarchy filters from man (ashraf al-makhluqat) to the Mumin to those who follow Ali and the Ahl al-Bayt; the perfect human (insan-e-kamil) in truth is the Imam, or by another perspective the Qa'im.
Religious truths exist in a world of relative perspectives (i'tibarat) where nothing said is the final word, which is why some acts are more excellent or forbidden depending on standpoint.

Din and dunya differ by a single alif in their letters, and that alif is the alif of ego (ana): when ego enters a person he becomes worldly (dunyadar), and religiosity (dindari) requires bowing the head in humility.

The esoteric meaning of ruku' is the Da'i (the hujjat), and the esoteric meaning of sajdah is the Imam and the Bab (his hujjat); so devoted was one Imam that the eighth Imam passed away in prostration.
When people called Ali 'Allah' and claimed he gives life, he insisted they regard him as a servant (bandah) and punished them by burning, the only one in history to give such a punishment.
The Arabic maxim 'man jadda wajada' (he who strives, finds) corresponds numerically to the abjad value of Ali (110), and no one strove harder than Ali.
Rajab is the seventh month and the month of Mawlana Ali, who is the seventh wasi and the Father of the Imams (Abu al-A'imma), the one from whom the counting of the Imams began.

In the word Mi'raj the letter mim stands for the Prophet and the letter 'ayn for Ali; on the night of ascension Ali was already present in the seventh heaven because Allah had created an angel in Ali's form.
Salawat upon the Prophet must always include the progeny (al), since the self (nafs) of the Prophet is Ali and mim and 'ayn are joined as 'ma'a' (with), always together.

Mim and 'ayn (the Prophet and Ali) effected the rescue of all the prophets — Yusuf from the well, Yunus from the fish, Nuh's boat — and guided every prophet throughout the period of concealment, so that their sovereignty rules the entire world.

The Prophet was given excellence from the perspectives of prophethood (nubuwwat), messengership (risalat), guardianship (walayat), speakership (natiqiyat), trusteeship (mustawda'), and permanent abode (mustaqarr).

The delicate task of religion is to maintain the exact relative rank between the Prophet and Ali — making Ali neither greater than nor lesser than his station — since the slightest error ruins the matter.

The hadith of al-Sadiq 'buna Allah al-Islam 'ala sab'i da'a'im: al-wilayah wa hiya afdaluhu wa biha wa bi'l-wali yusalu ila ma'rifatiha' establishes that Islam is built on seven pillars, that wilayah is the most excellent, and that through it and the wali one reaches gnosis.
The seven pillars of Islam are wilayah, taharah, salah, zakah, sawm, hajj, and jihad, and each is an esoteric parallel (mithl) of one of the speaking prophets.
The parallel of wilayah is Adam, because he was the first whose wilayah Allah made obligatory and to whom the angels were commanded to prostrate.
The angels commanded to prostrate to Adam were the noble hudud (mala'ikah bi'l-quwwah) present with Janab Hunayd, not unseen winged beings.
Prostration and obedience (al-sujud wa al-ta'ah) are themselves the wilayah, and faith in this wilayah is obligatory upon all creation.
The parallel of taharah is Nuh, the first prophet sent by Allah to purify the servants from the sins they committed after Adam, and the first Ulu al-'Azm prophet and first Natiq after Adam.

The water that effects purification is the sign of Nuh, and the flood is esoterically Janab Sam (Nuh's wasi) whose words of wisdom drowned the corrupt; such a destructive curse comes only from prophets, never from an Imam.
Nuh's actual lifespan was 120 years, while the figure of 900 years denotes the length of his era (dawr).
The parallel of salah is Ibrahim, who built the House as the qiblah and the Maqam as a place of prayer, with whom tawhid began, and who is in the embryonic stage of the clot (alaqah).

The Quranic verse 'wa-idh yarfa'u Ibrahimu al-qawa'id min al-bayt wa Isma'il rabbana taqabbal minna' refers esoterically to Ibrahim and Isma'il raising the foundations (qawa'id) of the chain of Imams in their progeny (Khayzar, Nabat, Salama).

The Prophet appointed his successors during his own life in sequence — Ali, then Hasan, then Husayn, then Ali Zayn al-'Abidin, then Muhammad al-Baqir — and naming an Imam Muhammad confers a special grace (wasilah).
The parallel of zakah is Musa, the first who called to Allah, indicated by the verse 'fa-qul hal laka ila an tazakka' (Would you purify yourself?).
Zakah is superior to fasting and always follows salah ('aqimu al-salah wa atu al-zakah'); establishing prayer is the Prophet and zakah is Ali, so purification is attained through the wilayah of Ali.

The parallel of sawm is 'Isa, the first whose mother (Maryam) was addressed; Maryam vowed a fast of silence ('inni nadhartu li'l-rahmani sawman fa-lan ukallima al-yawma insiyya'), and so fasting began in the time of 'Isa.

The parallel of hajj is Muhammad, the first to establish the rites and sunnah (manasik wa sunan), for though Hajj existed in jahiliyyah it was performed naked and without rites until the Prophet instituted them.

Pre-Islamic Arabs performed Hajj naked and 'their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping' (muka'an wa-tasdiyatan), and the Prophet forbade naked tawaf in his 'umrah performed before the conquest of Makkah.

The idols around the Ka'bah — Lat, 'Uzza, and Hubal — were originally venerated personalities (e.g. Lat a feudal landlord whose dependents made his idol after his death), and the Prophet and Ali together eradicated this shirk.
Hajj is the last of the obligatory deeds, and jihad is omitted from the list of deeds because jihad is not an action (amal) but a matter reserved for the hands of the Qa'im.

Jihad, the seventh pillar, is the parallel of the seventh Imam who appears in the seventh week — the forty-ninth week per the Dawr al-Tayyib, the week of the Resurrection — who is the Qa'im, the seventh of the nutafa' and the collective meeting-point (miqat majmu').

In the time of the Qa'im Allah gathers all people upon his command, and 'no one will oppose Islam and the limits of faith except that he be killed' (illa qatalahu) — killed for not following the shari'ah of Muhammad.
Allah gave Muhammad two additional excellences over all previous messengers, namely Hajj and Jihad.

In the time of the Qa'im, the Seal of the Imams, no faith is accepted — per 'yawma ya'ti ba'du ayati rabbika la yanfa'u nafsan imanuha lam takun amanat min qabl' — because the time for bringing faith ended with the Mahdi.

The transitional period in which faith can still be brought is the period of the Mahdi, figured as the interval between Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, and faith itself is wholly action (al-iman 'amalun kulluhu).

The same seven-pillar parallels recur within each week (uzbu') of Imams — the first like wilayah, second taharah, and so on — and the seventh of each week is named Mutimm just as Muhammad was named Khatim al-Anbiya'.

Muhammad ibn Isma'il is the seventh Imam, the Mutimm and Sab' al-Nutafa', with whom the first week of completers ends and from whom (via Isma'il) concealment began; the rank of speakership (natiqiyyah) reached him.
Mawlana Ahmad, the Sahib al-Uzbu', is both the 35th and 21st Imam, and although the master of two weeks (Uzbu'ayn) is greater than the master of one, Muhammad ibn Isma'il is greater than both.

The Five Pure Ones (Khamsat al-Athar) — Husayn, Hasan, Fatima, Ali, and the Prophet — are a special manifestation that dominates the eras (adwar), and Adam's repentance was accepted through their five names inscribed on the Throne (arsh).
Religion continued unbroken from Adam through Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa, with Musa and 'Isa being of lower rank than Ibrahim.

Ibrahim was made an Imam ('wa-ja'alna Ibrahim imama') and held the rank of close friendship (khullah) as Khalilullah, with the ranks of imamate accompanying him, though true Imamate proper did not come to him; his rank reached up to Qa'imiyyah.
The present period of concealment is the seventh and total era of concealment (satr kulli), the prior one having passed 57,000 years ago, and its structure is built to serve a 400,000-year era.
Just as the seven da'a'im are over the seven nutaqa', the week of the Imams begins with Hasan, and the seventh of the Imams corresponds to the seventh natiq, who is the Qa'im.

The Qa'im is the last of the Imams and the seventh of the speaking prophets, the collective meeting-point (miqat majmu') where the nutaqa', the ayimma, and the permanent and temporary ranks (mustaqirrin and mustawda'in) all converge and end.
The forty-ninth in the succession is the Imam, the fiftieth is the temporary one (mustawda', the Mahdi), and the fifty-first is the Qa'im.
The Mahdi stands in the parallel position (mahadh) of the Messenger and comes before the Qa'im, his paternal cousin, just as the Messenger came before Ali.

The stages of revelation map to the embryonic stages: sulala (Adam), nutfa (Nuh), 'alaqah (Ibrahim), continuing to lahm (the Prophet, sixth stage), with the blowing of the spirit (ruh) belonging to the Qa'im as the final stage.
The coming Mahdi's name will be Muhammad, completing the three M's: the first M (Prophet Muhammad), the middle M (Mahdi Billah, the eleventh Imam), and the last M (the coming Mahdi).

The Quranic allusion 'yawma ya'ti ba'du ayati rabbika la yanfa'u nafsan' applied to Saint Paul, who entered the era of 'Isa, originated the doctrine of the Trinity, and attempted to make 'Uzayr or 'Isa the son of God, after which intentions become frozen.

Azar, Ibrahim's maternal grandfather, denied and grew arrogant (ankara wastakbara) when Ibrahim presented his shari'ah, prompting Ibrahim's declaration 'hadha 'aduww Allah fa-tabarra'u minhu' (this is an enemy of God, disavow him).
Abu Bakr, unlike Azar, entered the da'wah but harbored the desire to succeed the Prophet, paralleling Saint Paul who entered 'Isa's era intending to corrupt it.
Ibrahim possesses the four ranks and is the unifier (jami') of the permanent and temporary lines, which he divided between Isma'il and Ishaq.
When a new prophet presents his shari'ah a division occurs and the real trouble arises (as in the time of Salman), and the call must first be presented within one's own house.
The eras have graded statuses by ordinal position, with 399 cycles (kawr) having passed and the present being the special 400th kawr, within a vast mawr period containing many dawr and athar.

The Panjatan Pak are the source of intercession (wasilah) for any need, being the constellation of Ali, Fatima, Hasan, Husayn, and the Prophet, and each of them holds a distinct collection or portfolio of mustaqarr and mustawda' parts.
The fifth position carries special importance, since Husayn is the fifth of the Panjatan, so that every fifth rank holds significance.

Ja'far al-Sadiq is the fifth of the Imams and the fifth of the completers, connected to the fifth natiq 'Isa (who gave life and special knowledge), and the Da'a'im al-Islam emerged from Ja'far al-Sadiq and al-Baqir.
Al-Baqir is the fourth Imam, holding the special rank of the sun, and the command 'ya Baqir, ibqar al-'ilm baqran' (O Baqir, split open knowledge thoroughly) names his function of opening knowledge.

The Da'a'im al-Islam is the basic shari'ah that will remain in force until the Resurrection, changeable only by the Qa'im, who will lift the obligatory deeds (a'mal-i taklifiyyah) when the period of concealment ends.

At the coming of the Qa'im the test is of what one studied and did in the era of Muhammad: passing earns reward and failing earns death, and 'innama al-a'malu bi-l-niyyat' means a deed is valid only if its intention is right.
In Surah al-Haqqah the believer's wish 'ya laytani kuntu turaban' means he wishes he had become a believer, since turab (dust) is the final and saving element-stage.

The Quranic image 'yatluju al-jamalu fi samm al-khiyat' (the camel through the eye of the needle) means that the whole world must eventually shrink its arrogance and pass through the blessed foot (pa-i sharif) of Ali by believing in him.
There is no compulsion in the da'wah ('I give you my hand; take it if you will'), so one comes by his own will, and many do not come by their own stubbornness.

Everything returns to its origin, the earth, and since the wasi of the Prophet (Ali) stands in the station of the earth while the sky is the natiq, all souls must by a natural force come to Ali as objects fall by gravity.

Intentions were shuffled during the descent (from grateful to insistent to repentant), and once a soul arrived in a given state its intention is fixed and not afterward changed, so each returns in its own time with its own intention.
The community does not engage in forced preaching (tabligh) like the Tablighi Jamaat; it only explains, leaving acceptance to the listener without compulsion.
The second question of the discourse asks whether the acts of worship (taharah, salah, zakah, sawm, hajj) have a meaning and wisdom behind them, and if not, how they differ from any other action.

The Prophet incorporated the obligatory acts (a'mal-e-taklifiyyah) into the shari'ah system to eliminate the believer's shortcomings (qusurat) from the fall, this being a requirement of the era of concealment.
The obligations of wudu (fara'id) come from Allah while its recommended practices (sunan), such as rinsing the mouth and nose, came later from the Imam.

The Quranic wudu command 'faghsilu wujuhakum wa aydiyakum wamsahu bi-ru'usikum wa arjulakum' is the most true (asdaq), requiring the face and hands to be washed and the head and feet to be wiped (masah), not washed.
Washing the head or feet instead of wiping them invalidates the wudu, the rationale being that masah uses less water and ghusl more, so water is applied in proportion to need.
The obligation of wudu rests on four limbs — the face, the two hands, the head, and the two feet.
The face in wudu is the parallel of the Natiq of the Era (the Face of Allah, wajhullah), who in this cycle is Muhammad bin 'Abdullah.
A Natiq is defined as the one whose speech silences all others, who remain in the position of the silent (samit).
Washing the face esoterically signifies acknowledgment (iqrar) of the Natiq, obedience (ta'at) to him, and acting (amal) upon what he brought.
The two hands in wudu are the parallel of the Imam and his Hujjat, and washing them signifies acknowledgment and obedience of both; the term Hujjat denotes the coming khalifa (Imam al-Zaman).

The head (ra's) in wudu is the parallel of the Natiq, chief of the entire world (ra'is al-alam), since the head of every thing is its highest and most excellent part, and wiping it signifies acknowledgment and adherence to the shari'ah (iltizam).
The three-part wiping of the head represents the three confidants (salasa sufara') — Mawlana 'Abd al-Muttalib, Janab 'Abdullah, and Janab Abu Talib — who are the powers of the brain.
The two feet (rijlan) in wudu are the parallel of the Imam and the Hujjat (or the Wasi, the shin/saq pertaining to Ali al-Murtada), and wiping them signifies acknowledgment of both.
The water that purifies outward impurities is the parallel of the knowledge taken from the people of truth (ahl al-haqq), by which souls are purified and the sciences of the esoteric are held.

Washing the front (qubul) and the back (dubur) signifies purification from polytheism (shirk) and disbelief (kufr) respectively, shirk being the greater evil of not believing in Allah at all and kufr the lesser of turning back after Islam.

The passing of wind (rih) signifies hypocrisy (nifaq), which like a hidden hypocrite is imperceptible; Sayyidna 'Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Makrami ruled that ablution of the private parts (abdas) is required even upon passing wind.
Nifaq is etymologically a tunnel (nafaq), denoting one who lets what enters one ear exit the other, going in and turning back out.

The inner reality (al-wudu al-batin) of wudu is the respondent's acknowledgment before the Da'i Mutlaq when taking the covenant ('ahd), affirming all the hudud above him and disavowing (bara'ah) their opposites.

The right hand parallels the Ma'zun and the left hand the Mukasir; ablution of the private parts (abdas) is done only with the left hand because the Mukasir, of lower rank, is the one who can break and stop matters at the lower level.
The reward of an act is proportional to the worshipper's understanding of its meaning, and the difference between mere washing of the hands and wudu lies in meaning and intention (niyyat).

Pouring water on the palate (talu), the most sensitive part of the body, produces a shiver that is an awakening for prayer, corresponding esoterically to the rank of Mawlana 'Abd al-Muttalib (the jaddayn).
The contemporary awakening and unveiling of realities (kashf al-haqaiq) is the blessing of the present Imam, the grandfather of the Qa'im (Sa'ib al-'Asr, Mawlana Muhammadin 'Ali).

Though the Imam of the Time is in concealment, all worldly guidance, revolutions, and the very ability to speak and worship flow from him, expressed in the poem that names him the sun of the age (aftab-e-waqt) from whom others take light.

The Prophet stands in the station of the sun and Ali in the station of the moon, and after their passing the Imam and his Hujjat (the Da'i) hold those stations, with light filtering downward from the Da'i to the Ma'zuns and below.
Ziya is the light of the sun, which the Da'i receives, and nur is the light of the moon, which the believers receive in filtered form.
What is gifted from above (mawhub) is not in one's control, but what is earned (kasab) must be pursued to the last breath, so that even a great scholar remains a student (talib-e-ilm).
Tonight combines three virtues: the Night of Ascension (Shab-e-Mi'raj), the birth (wiladat) of Amir al-Mu'minin, and the commissioning (bi'that) of the Prophet.
The Ka'batullah's special blessing is the spot called Rukhamat al-Hamra, where the dome was first built, where the world began, and where every Hajj al-Da'iyyah takes place.
The Prophet's first proclamation was 'Qulu La ilaha illa-llah tuflihu', and Islam began on the peaks of Faran when the Prophet reached the age of maturity at forty.

The hadith 'Kuntu Nabiyyan wa Adamu bayn al-ma'i wa-t-tin' (I was a Prophet when Adam was between water and clay) means the Prophet held prophethood already when Adam was in the stages of shari'ah and ta'wil.
The foundational ranks ascend from Nabi to Risalat to Natiqiyyat to the Ulul 'Azm prophets to the rank of Khullat, and the Prophet attained ranks above all of them.

The days of the week are assigned to the prophets — Adam to Sunday, Nuh to Monday, and so on — so that Friday belongs to the Prophet (because it gathers, jama') and Saturday (Sabt) to the Qa'im, and the Prophet's major events occurred on Mondays.

The Prophet taught 'Man qala La ilaha illa-llah mukhlisan dakhala-l-jannah' and defined the sincerity (ikhlas) as 'ada'u huquqiha wa ma'rifatu hududiha' — fulfilling its rights (the pillars) and knowing its limits (the hudud).
Paradise is a relative term with graded levels (jannat-e-'aliyat), distinguishing an Islamic paradise from an Imani paradise.

After death the believer's base matter (fuzlaat) is conveyed from the grave through the mosque's prayer niche (mihrab), the miqat, the bata'iq, to the channel of mercy (mizab-e-rahmat), transforming from dhakha'ir to khama'ir to zubad.

The believer's noble substance, raised from the twelve islands, ascends to the sphere of the constellations (falak-e-buruj, the eighth sphere above Saturn), where the twelve islands correspond to the twelve constellations and undergo dissolution (tahlil), purification (tasfiyah), and refinement (tanqih).

The believer's substance spends 280 years in the grave and 720 years above, after which the inherent essence (jawharat-e-gharizi) descends, turns toward the vegetative soul (nafs-e-namiyah), and density converts into subtlety.

The root of ikhlas is khalasa (khay-lam-sad, numerically 720), suggesting that a perfect believer completes his refinement in 720 years and returns with one part reduced, since success requires being reduced.
Ibrahim spread the first mass tawhid and stands in the mansion of the clot ('alaqah), from which the original connection of the sperm is born.

Hanif al-Kindi narrated in the books of Siyar that he saw the Prophet, Khadijah, and Ali praying secretly while Islam was hidden, and later regretted not accepting Islam then to become the second after Ali.

On the night of Hijrat, when the tribes conspired to kill the Prophet with one young man from each tribe, Ali slept in the Prophet's bed wearing his green sheet as an act of obedience and self-sacrifice.

The Prophet recited the opening verses of Surah Yasin ('wa ja'alna min bayni aydihim saddan wa min khalfihim saddan fa-aghshaynahum fa-hum la yubsiroon'), threw dust, and walked out unseen by the conspirators.

The true circle of Iman begins with the appointment (nass) of Mawlana Ali, which Allah commanded the Prophet to make through 'Balligh ma unzila ilayk' with the assurance 'Wallahu ya'simuka min an-nas'.
The three Hajj types — Qiran, Mufrad, and Tamattu' bi-l-'Umrah — were performed by the Prophet one per year, and returning from the final Hajj he proclaimed 'man kuntu mawlahu fa-'Aliyyun mawlahu'.

In the 'Ashura prayer the salvation of every prophet — Nuh's ark reaching Judi, Ibrahim's deliverance from the fire, and the rest — is attributed to the working of the mukhtari veil and the karrari veil, namely the Prophet (mim) and Ali ('ayn), the two luminaries (nayyirayn).
The sovereignty (raj) of mim and 'ayn over the entire world of humanity until the Day of Judgment is itself the Mi'raj.

In the verse 'Subhana-lladhi asra bi-'abdihi laylan min al-Masjid al-Haram ila al-Masjid al-Aqsa', asra means the Prophet's walking from Makkah to Aqsa, and the Mi'raj proper is the ascent from the rock (Sakhrah) at Masjid al-Aqsa.

On the Mi'raj the fifty prayers were reduced to five at Musa's counsel, and at the station 'dana fa-tadalla fa-kana qaba qawsayni aw adna' the Prophet found Ali already seated, an angel having been created in Ali's form for the angels' longing.
The saying 'Muhammadun wa 'Aliyyun khayr al-bashar' (Muhammad and Ali are the best of mankind) expresses the joint rank the Prophet attained.

The ranks of knowledge ascend from haqa'iq to daqa'iq to the lofty hidden things (khafiya-e-'aliyah) to the daqa'iq al-daqa'iq, and the outpourings (ifazat) of a great person — even two words — are plundered jewels.
Amir al-Mu'minin was born at Mustajar when the wall of the Ka'bah split and Mawlatina Fatima bint Asad entered, emerging with the child.
The Prophet was granted ascending ranks marked by revelation — the ninth rank with Surah Taha and the tenth rank when Yasin became his address — having traversed many ranks in twenty-three years.

The verse 'Wa la ta'kulu mimma lam yudhkari-smullahi 'alayh' obliges every person not to eat that over which Allah's name has not been mentioned, because invoking the name removes the harmful things present in the food.
Ali taught Ibn al-Kawwa' that one must say Bismillah over every type of food ('ala kulli naw'), since saying it over one type does not cover the others.
Per Sayyidna 'Ali bin Sulayman, a man in a state of impurity and a woman in menstruation, who may not recite the Quran, may still say Bismillah since taking Allah's name is not reciting a verse.
Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan would summon people to food by saying 'Sammu' (say Bismillah) rather than 'come to eat'.
Exoterically, zakat is taking a portion from the wealth of the rich to the one in authority (wali al-amr) so that he may distribute it among the poor according to their classes.
Zakat has eight categories of recipients — faqir, miskin, yatim, asir, mu'allafati'l-qulub, and the collectors ('ummal) — where a faqir is one who asks and a miskin one whose poverty is evident.

The esoteric meaning of zakat is the imparting of knowledge by the beneficial scholars ('ulama'-i mufidin, the wealthy in knowledge) to the students (mustafidin) under them, the senior teaching the junior from a rank above.

It is not permissible to give zakat directly to the poor; it must be handed upward to the Master of the Age (wali al-amr) for proper distribution, per the verse 'khudh min amwalihim sadaqatan tutahhiruhum wa tuzakkihim biha'.

By clear text (nass) zakat is delivered to the Prophet, then to whoever stands in his place from the Imams in every era, then the Da'i, then those below — and esoterically no one may teach his knowledge except by the permission of the wali al-zaman, the owner and treasurer of knowledge.
Exoterically, fasting (sawm) is abstaining (imsak) from eating, drinking, and intercourse during the day, made obligatory only in the month of Ramadan.

The esoteric meaning of fasting is abstaining from speaking of the ta'wil to the people of the exoteric da'wah (the counterpart of day/nahar), while the manifestation of ta'wil to one's own people occurs at night (layl) and is the counterpart of iftar.
Ramadan being the ninth month is the parallel of the Wasi (Ali), who is the ninth wasi.

Ali is the ninth wasi by this count: Adam had two (Habil and Shith), Nuh one (Sam), Ibrahim two (Isma'il and Ishaq), Musa two (Harun and Yusha'), 'Isa two (Sham'un al-Safa and another), so the wasi of the natiq of the cycle is the ninth.

Isma'il's rank is greater as owner of the imamah while Ishaq held prophethood (nubuwwah), though a portion of successorship (wasayah) was also given to Ishaq, and the matter of the sacrifice (zabh) carries deep realities.
All descendants of Ishaq are servants (khadim) of Isma'il and his progeny, whose established line (mustaqarrin) they serve, though Ishaq also held prophethood and messengership.

The first division in the world occurred in the time of Ibrahim (and later 'Abd al-Muttalib), where Lut was given a share, ranked after Isma'il as the holder of the qasim and before Ishaq's prophethood.

For roughly 3000 years from Ibrahim to the Prophet, prophethood continued through the Bani Isra'il (descendants of Ishaq in Lebanon and Syria) with Musa and 'Isa under the oppressed (mustad'afin), until the line was reassembled in the time of 'Abd al-Muttalib.

The divisions serve to sort the juniors (sughara'), gathered in the starry assembly (tanjumi majma') traced to Mawlana Tanjum (Adam bin Tanjum) before Adam, all destined to converge in the Qa'im as the appointed gathering (miqat al-majmu').

Fasting in the ninth month signifies the concealment (kitman) of the knowledge of the Wasi — the esoteric, divine sciences — which must be hidden until permission to reveal is granted, the revelation having begun in the time of Sayyid Humam.
The ta'wil of the thirty days of fasting is the thirty years the Wasi (Ali) remained silent and hidden after the Prophet by Allah's command, though he was a brave warrior who could have acted.

The thirty days of fasting are the parallel of the Wasi's hudud established with esoteric knowledge — the ten Imams of his progeny with their hujaj and abwab — and the iftar/'Id signifies the eleventh, Imam 'Abdullah al-Mahdi, who manifests the famous da'wah.
Waiting for 'Id signifies waiting for the Mahdi, who stands in the station of dawn (fajr), since the moon rises only after the sun sets — Ali's era beginning only at the Prophet's last time.
Exoterically, Hajj is the intention (qasd) to go to the Sacred House, and esoterically it is the recognition (ma'rifat) of the Imam of the time and adherence to his covenant ('ahd).

Donning ihram at the miqat with ablution and two white unstitched garments (izar and rida') signifies that one entering the da'wah of truth must purify himself from the garment of sins before his da'i who takes the covenant.
The miqat (the boundary far from the Ka'bah) is the parallel of the da'i from whom the covenant is taken, while the Imam stands in the station of the Hajj (the Ka'bah).

The prohibition of a stitched garment (mukhayyat) in ihram signifies abandoning (rafz) the matters of the exoteric and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y), the two white garments standing for the sound exoteric and the esoteric per the people of truth.
Analogical reasoning (qiyas) is the creation of 'Umar's religion, and 'the first to use analogical reasoning was Iblis' (awwalu man qasa Iblis).
In the tawaf the House (bayt) is the parallel of the Imam and the Black Stone (hajar) in the corner is the parallel of the Imam's Hujjat.

Circumambulating the House signifies adhering to the da'wah of the Imam of the time (who stands in the station of the natiq), and kissing the Stone signifies taking from his Hujjat, enacted in the supplication 'allahumma inni usafihuhu' (shaking hands with the da'wah).
The tawaf is the parallel of acknowledging the seven nutaqa' (six having passed and the seventh being the Qa'im), since everything proceeds in sevens — weeks, periods, and cycles of concealment.
Touching the Stone (istilam al-hajar) signifies submitting (taslim) to the command of the Imam's Hujjat and being bound (iltizam) to the da'i.
The two rak'ah of tawaf at the Maqam signify establishing both the exoteric (zahir) and the esoteric (batin) of the religion.

In the sa'y between Safa and Marwa, Safa is the parallel of the mufid (the beneficial one) and Marwa the parallel of the hadd al-mufid (the rank above the mufid from whom the command comes), with Safa's rank being the greater.

The things of the established ones (mustaqarrin) are near the Ka'bah while the things of the oppressed (mustad'afin) are at Safa and Marwa, and the running between them signifies the respondent's connection (ittisal) with his teacher and his teacher's leader to progress in ranks of knowledge.
The stoning of the three pillars (ramy al-jimar) signifies the three great ones of the community who led it astray, and throwing pebbles signifies invalidating their imamate with proofs (hujaj).
The slaughter on the Day of Sacrifice (al-nahr fi yawm al-nahr) signifies the killing of the opponents (addad) who will stand before the Qa'im, who is himself an example of the Day of Sacrifice.

The Quranic water that purifies in the time of Nuh is esoterically the knowledge ('ilm) of the wasi Janab Sam (the tannur/oven from which the flood gushed), since the streams of knowledge always emerge from the side of the wasi.
Believing in Ali is insufficient; one must believe in the entire progeny (zurriyat) of Imams without leaving out even one, or one's tawhid is finished.

The three M's — 'awwaluna Muhammad, awsatuna Muhammad, wa-akhiruna Muhammad' — are the Prophet, the eleventh Imam Mahdi of Egypt, and the coming Mahdi, with the coming Mahdi in the mansion of the Prophet and the Qa'im in the mansion of Ali, making Ali a partial Qa'im (Qa'im-i juzwi).
The Qa'im is the final foundation (asaas), so two foundations (asaasain) are established — Ali as the asaas of the natiq and the Qa'im as the foundation of the coming Mahdi.

The Qa'im has no ummah, being a concluding figure who is not a possessor of a shari'ah, and since each new shari'ah abrogates the prior, only the Qa'im can abrogate the shari'ah of Muhammad and lift the religious obligations (takalif) when the period of concealment ends.

The jihad of the Qa'im is enacted at the three gates of Mina — Bab al-Jamal (camel), Bab al-Ghanam (sheep), and Bab al-Baqar (cattle) — where he slaughters the great opponents like Pharaoh and Nimrod by his own hand and assigns the lesser ones to those below him.

The Qa'im is the 51st in rank while the present Imam is the 48th and the sixth of his week (his son being the seventh), yet the present Imam's importance is greater in the manner of a grandfather, as 'Abd al-Muttalib's importance exceeded Abu Talib's.
In rank a grandfather exceeds a father, so just as 'Abd al-Muttalib exceeded Abu Talib, the father of the Qa'im (Abu'l-Qa'im) exceeds the present Qa'im.

The first week (usbu') of Imams runs from Hasan through Muhammad ibn Isma'il, stands in the mansion of wilayah, is the most excellent of all weeks, and contains all the highest-ranking Imams (the jewels).

The master of two weeks (sahib-i usbu'ain) exceeds the master of one week, with Mawlana Tayyib (21st Imam) and Mawlana Ahmad (35th Imam) being sahib-i usbu'ain, yet Muhammad ibn Isma'il, master of only one week, remains the greatest of all.

Mawlana Ahmad is also the master of the era (sahib-i dawr) one thousand years after the Prophet, and Sayyidna Humam announced the da'wat exactly at the millennium (the era beginning in 970), since each natiq is given a thousand years to make seven natiqs' 7000 years of concealment.

Al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq spread the shari'ah of Muhammad ('Ya Baqir al-'ilm'), and miracles (karamat) occurred in the time of Ja'far al-Sadiq, the fifth Imam, paralleling the fifth natiq 'Isa who was a source of miracles.

'Isa had three veils (hijab) — Armiya, Yahya, and Yusuf — who bore the crucifixion, since per 'wa-ma qataluhu wa-ma salabuhu wa-lakin shubbiha lahum' 'Isa was neither killed nor crucified but made to resemble another.

Husayn, the last of the Khamsat al-Athar and the parallel of the fifth natiq, had three veils — Hani, Muslim ibn 'Aqil, and 'Abbas (the greatest, at the end) — each lower one serving as a veil for the higher and all of them veils for Husayn.

The fourth rank carries the power of nurturing (quwwat-i tarbiyyah, from rabi'/the sun) and the seventh carries the power of counting (quwwat-i tasbi', from sabi'/the moon), since the sun begins and the moon completes.

The embryonic stages map to the prophets and their faculties: sulalah (Adam), nutfah (Nuh), 'alaqah (Ibrahim, where life and tawhid begin), the fourth Musa (kalimullah, power of nurturing, when movement begins), 'izam/bones ('Isa), lahm/flesh (the Prophet, 'fa-kasawna'l-'izama lahman'), and the blowing of the spirit (the Qa'im).

All souls — Musa's people, 'Isa's people, and all others — will gather with the Qa'im at the appointed gathering (miqat al-majmu') like rivers falling into a great ocean, though the perfection of religion occurred in the time of the Prophet.

The verse 'al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum wa-atmamtu 'alaykum ni'mati' marks the completion of religion, and the favor (ni'mat) being completed is Ali, the greatest favor, since the mention of the four favors is the mention of Ali.
